en: The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai explains the passage "neither distant nor near" in three parts: first, a general indication of the object and wisdom; second, a detailed explanation;
and third, a concluding synthesis. "Contemplation" (guan) refers to the contemplative wisdom of the Middle Way; "all phenomena" (sarvadharma) refers to the ten dharma-realms.

This refers to the objective realm (*viṣaya*). If one were to discuss wisdom (*jñāna*) alone, wisdom would have nothing to contemplate; therefore, "all" is mentioned to reveal that everything is empty.
The term "as it truly is" (*yathābhūtam*) follows as a separate explanation.

The two extremes and the three truths are neither one nor different; thus it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Because it is not [attained through] the seven stages of expedient means, it is called "Reality" (*bhūta*); because its characteristic is reality, it is termed the "True Suchness Aspect" (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*).
"Non-perverted" means being free from the eight inversions.
"Immovable" means not being moved by the two types of death.
"Non-retrogressive" means that with each thought-moment entering into quiescence, one enters the ocean of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
"Non-revolution" means not revolving in birth and death like ordinary beings, nor revolving through the stages of ordinary and sagehood like those of the Two Vehicles.

"Like space" means that there is only a name, yet the name cannot be apprehended; likewise, the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation also exists only as a name, and when sought, it cannot be apprehended.
"Non-existence of anything whatsoever" means the absence of a nature that is self-originated, other-originated, co-originated, or causeless.
"The cessation of all paths of verbal expression" means it is inconceivable.
"Non-arising" means that both afflictions and wisdom are fundamentally non-arising in principle.
"Non-emergence" means that what the Tathāgata has remedied shall never again manifest.
"Non-arising" means that all skillful means are utterly quiescent.
"Namelessness" means that names cannot name it.
"Signlessness" means that signs cannot characterize it.
"Non-existence" (anupalambha) means the absence of existence in either of the two extremes.
"Immeasurable" (apramāṇa) means it is not a quantifiable phenomenon.
"Boundless" (ananta) means it has no spatial location.
"Unobstructed and unimpeded" means pervading all places.
"Existing only through causes and conditions" is the conclusion.

Above, the contemplative wisdom of the Middle Way was directly elucidated; now, the simultaneous illumination of the two extremes is clarified. The principle-nature is ultimately pure as previously described—neither liberation nor delusion—and yet, from the causes and conditions of delusion, birth and death arise; from the causes and conditions of liberation, nirvana arises.

Furthermore, because of causes and conditions, existence exists within nirvana; that which arises from inversion gives rise to birth-and-death—this is the explicit meaning of the simultaneous illumination of both [aspects].
"Constantly and joyfully contemplating such dharmas as these" refers precisely to the dharmas of the three truths and so forth.
Furthermore, the phrase "arising from inversion solely through causes and conditions" concludes the inconceivable realm of the three truths.
The phrase "therefore it is said" refers to the inconceivable teaching.
"Constantly observing with joy" refers to the synthesis of the three inconceivable contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, "observing all phenomena as empty and of suchness" indicates the essence of the contemplation;
"not being inverted and departing from the nine propositions" explains the characteristics of the contemplation.
To be unmoved by the two extremes or the eight inversions is called "non-inverted and immovable";
to not fall into the two stages of the two vehicles or ordinary beings is why it is said to be "non-retrogressive and non-reversing."
These two lines clarify the application of principle through wisdom:

because it is not of the future, it does not arise; because it is not of the past, it does not emerge; because it is not of the present, it does not originate. As the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Śāstra-vyākhyā), fascicle 51, states: "Like space, it has no characteristic of entering, no characteristic of emerging, and no characteristic of abiding. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is likewise: there is no place of entry in the future, no place of emergence in the past, and no place of abiding in the present.
The forty-third [section] states: "Not arising from the side of causes is called 'not emerging'; not arising from the side of conditions is called 'unborn'.
There are nineteen phrases in total; the first phrase is general, while the subsequent eighteen correspond to the eighteen emptinesses (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The true mark of reality is the emptiness of the ultimate meaning;
non-perversion is internal emptiness, for internally there are no six sense bases, nor self or what belongs to a self;
non-perversion and immovability are external emptiness, for externally one is not moved by the six sense objects.
"Non-retrogression" refers to internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*); because the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are empty, it is called non-retrogression.

"Non-turning" refers to the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Emptiness destroys all phenomena: all phenomena are that which is destroyed, while emptiness is that which destroys. When there are no longer any phenomena and only emptiness remains, and this emptiness itself is also empty, it is called the "emptiness of emptiness.
Since emptiness is already empty, there is nothing further that can turn; therefore, it is called non-turning.
That which is like space is the great emptiness;
it is said to be "like space" because it is free from the conceptualization of directions and their boundaries.
The nature of non-existence is ultimate emptiness.
Because all phenomena are without remainder, they are called "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*);

because of this ultimate emptiness, they have the nature of non-existence. All paths of verbal expression are severed, which is itself universal emptiness; because universal emptiness cannot be spoken of, the paths of verbal expression are severed.

Non-arising is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*); the conditioned is a conjunction of causes and conditions, and since there is no such conjunction, there is no arising. Non-emergence is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
Namelessness is transcendence; because the phenomena of transcendence are empty, it is called "non-transcendence.
Non-arising is beginningless emptiness, for an original beginning cannot be found, and thus there is no arising.
Namelessness is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, which can be understood.
The signless is the emptiness of signs;
that which is truly non-existent is the emptiness of the unapprehendable;
the immeasurable is the emptiness of existing phenomena.
Where there is a phenomenon (*dharma*), there is measure; since that which has measure is empty, it is said to be immeasurable and boundless, which means the emptiness of non-phenomena (*adharma*).
Non-phenomena constitute a limit (*anta*); because they are now empty, they are boundless and unimpeded—this is the emptiness of both phenomena and non-phenomena.

Because neither of these two can be apprehended, it is called "unimpeded. Being without obstruction is "dispersed emptiness" (*vibhava-śūnyatā*); because hindrances cannot be apprehended, it is called "without obstruction."
The eighteen kinds of emptiness are all the Middle Way and right wisdom; they are all termed "emptiness," and are spoken of as "eighteen" only because they correspond to eighteen types of objects.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states, "Because the Tathāgata constantly cultivates the meaning of the eighteen kinds of emptiness. Thus, the eighteen kinds of emptiness are employed here to explain the eighteen phrases.
The verses consist of twenty-eight lines of three phrases each, divided into three parts:
first, one line in verse summarizes the headings;
next, twenty-two lines in verse describe the practice.
The subsequent five lines and three phrases clarify the accomplishment of practice.

While the prose explains the long-term practice in detail and provides a specific interpretation, the verses condense these into stanzas; thus, although the explicit words differ, their underlying meaning is identical, as the expanded and abbreviated expositions manifest through mutual inclusion and exclusion, providing an even more reliable basis for understanding.

In the preceding section, there were three items each for the two categories of "superior practice" and "proximate practice. Now, in this verse, they are combined into a single summary and no longer follow their original sequence.

First, the fourteen lines beginning with "should enter into practice" summarize the distance of the objects; whereas above there were ten types of distancing, these are omitted here and not in order, as can be seen from the text itself.

This also versifies the practice of the emptiness of persons; taking its essential meaning, it simultaneously versifies the three meanings of the "near practices. Therefore, the verse says: "This is what is called the practice and the near practice."
Regarding the phrase "always staying away from kings," there are ten unrighteous matters concerning a bhikṣu’s intimacy with a king:

first, plotting against the king’s life; second, the king’s execution of a high minister; third, the loss of treasures from the treasury; fourth, a woman of the palace being pregnant; fifth, the king’s body being poisoned; sixth, strife and rivalry among high ministers; seventh, two nations engaging in war; eighth, the king being stingy and failing to bestow gifts upon the people; ninth, the levying of taxes from the people’s goods; and tenth, the prevalence of many epidemics—wherein it is said that the bhikṣu performs incantations.

When these ten matters exist, all ministers and subjects will attribute them to the actions of the bhikṣu; by thus slandering the bhikṣu, they simultaneously slander the Dharma and the Buddha. Therefore, the Buddha does not permit [bhikṣus] to associate closely with kings.
Regarding "non-Buddhist brahmins," the *Madhyama Āgama* states: "The first person was named Brahmā, who created one Veda.
Next came Śukra, who divided the one into four: first, the Veda of Recitation;
second, the Veda of Sacrifice; third, the Veda of Chanting; and fourth, the Veda of Averting Calamities."
Each [of these] consisted of three hundred and twenty thousand verses, totaling one million two hundred and eighty thousand verses, comprising one thousand seven hundred fascicles.
Next was Puṣya, who had twenty-five disciples; each was able to extensively analyze one Veda, and thus there came to be twenty-five Vedas.
Next, there was a man named Śuka who transformed one Veda into eighteen.
Next, there was a man named Sudharmā who had twenty-one disciples; he transformed [the Veda] into twenty-one Vedas.
"In this manner, it was successively transformed into the twelve hundred and six Vedas.
The *Veda* (毘陀) treatises—here translated as "Treatises on Wisdom" (*Jñāna-śāstra*)—were composed by Vyāsa and consist of four types:
first, the *Śruti-veda*, which clarifies the ritual worship of fire and the extinction of sins;...
2. Yajurveda, which clarifies that making offerings to Brahmins brings merit;
3. Sāmaveda, which clarifies the reconciliation of two nations;
4. Atharvaveda, which clarifies warfare.
Having studied these four treatises, he claimed to be an omniscient person (*sarvajña*).
Vyākaraṇa—here translated as "Grammar"—was composed by Pāṇini; it elucidates various scriptures as well as diverse colloquial dialects.

The Vaiśeṣika treatise was composed by Ulūka, which translates as "Most Victorious" (Jiasheng); he appeared eight hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and elucidated the six truths (*ṣat-tattva*).

Kapila, which translates as "Yellow-Headed" (Huangtou) or "Turtle-Lineage" (Guizhong), composed a treatise named Sāṃkhya; *Sāṃkhya* means "Countless" (Wuding). Because the treatise is named after its author, it is called Kapila, and he expounded twenty-five truths (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*).
Regarding "the scholars of the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna": when the Buddha was at Vārāṇasī, he first taught the Sūtra Piṭaka for the sake of the five bhikṣus;
when the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, he first taught the Vinaya Piṭaka for the sake of Sunakṣatra;
and when the Buddha was at the Markaṭahrada in Vaiśālī, he first taught the Abhidharma Piṭaka for the sake of the son of the Vaṅgas.

At the first watch of the night, five hundred arhats assembled to compile the Abhidharma Piṭaka, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; this constitutes the study of the Tripiṭaka. Regarding the phrase "deeply attached to the five desires," as for the characteristics of desire:

among the people of the four continents, the nāgas, the asuras, and the Four Heavenly Kings, they all engage through the contact of their sense organs. In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they take the wind as their activity; in the Yāma Heaven, they take proximity as their activity; in the Tuṣita Heaven, they take mutual attraction as their activity; in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, they take gazing at one another as their activity; and in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, they take mental conception as their activity. Those in the higher heavens are all free from desire.
Regarding the phrase "widows and virgins," Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, how should one regard women?
The Buddha said:
"Do not meet with them; if you do meet them, do not speak with them; if you must speak with them, you should focus your mind single-mindedly on the Buddha.
Regarding "those who are not male," they are called *paṇḍaka*, which here is translated as *huanmen* (eunuch).
"Yellow-gate attendants" (eunuchs) are those who possess both male and female forms but are incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse.

Regarding "entering a village to beg for food," the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "There was once a sheep that went to a dung heap, ate its fill, and returned to the flock, boasting, 'I have obtained excellent food. Monks are also like this: having received the four requisites, they give rise to thoughts of defiled attachment and do not know the essential way out; even if they do not receive them, they constantly harbor such thoughts, and if they do receive them, they become arrogant toward other monks and disparage others, saying, 'I have obtained what they could not obtain. This is called the 'sheep-like monk begging for food.'"

When the lion king encounters a large beast, he devours it without savoring its taste or becoming attached; when he catches a small beast, he devours it without contempt or disdain. It is the same for the bhikṣu:

when he receives the four requisites of support, he does not give rise to defiled attachment or thoughts of desire, knowing for himself the way to transcendence. Even if he does not obtain offerings, he does not give rise to distracted thoughts or a mind of fluctuation—neither increase nor decrease. This is the alms-round of the lion-king bhikṣu.

Regarding the four matters of begging for food, traveling, labor, and illness, there are eight periods—four before and four after—which clarify eight instances of diligence and eight instances of indolence.
Before begging for food, one forms this thought: "I do this to cultivate the Way and mend the wounds of hunger"; thus, even if food has not yet been obtained, one does not abandon mindful practice.
Once food has been obtained, one continues without ceasing to mindfully contemplate the Way out of gratitude; during these two periods, before and after, one redoubles one's diligence.
The other three matters are likewise in their sequence; the opposite of these is called the eight forms of indolence.
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* clarifies that alms-food should be divided into four portions:

one portion to be offered to fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*), one portion to be given to beggars, one portion to be bestowed upon spirits and deities, and one portion to be consumed by oneself.

"Furthermore, they do not practice" and below is the second section, consisting of eight lines, which praises the principle that is neither distant nor near, being situated at the point where distance and proximity coincide.
"If there is a bhikṣu" and below is the third section, consisting of five lines and three phrases, clarifying the accomplishment of practice; this is further divided into three parts:
the first one and a half lines mark the accomplishment of practice.
When the practice is perfected, external deportment is without error; when the principle is perfected, the inner mind is without obstruction. Thus it is said, "without timidity.
Next, from "At times, the Bodhisattva... onwards, is the second section: through the perfection of the three practices, one attains peace and happiness.

Following this, one line and one verse summarize the preceding prose. From "The Bodhisattva enters the quiet chamber" onwards, the causes of peace and happiness are explained. By practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one ceases transgressions and evils;

thus, having attained the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), one is not harmed externally. By practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one becomes free from all grasping and attachment; thus, having attained the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), there is no inversion internally. This is what it means for the mind not to be timid or weak; this lack of timidity is called peace and happiness.
Below the section on “Mañjuśrī,” the third part consists of one line and one phrase, which summarizes the prose section.
Second, regarding the "Peaceful Practice of Speech," there is also both prose and verse.
The long exposition consists of two parts:
first, the presentation of the headings; second, the explanation of the methods of practice.
The presentation of the headings is as stated in the text.
From "If one proclaims with the mouth" below, the practice of the Dharma is explained, which further divides into two:
namely, the practice of tranquility (śamatha) and the practice of insight (vipaśyanā). The practice of tranquility consists of four parts:
First, not speaking of faults; second, not being contemptuous; third, not disparaging; fourth, not harboring resentment.
Regarding the first—those who do not delight in speaking of others' transgressions—if people listen for faults, what fault could there be in the Dharma?

The seven stages of expedient means are the Buddha’s teachings spoken in accordance with the inclinations of others; they are called "provisional" (neyārtha). If one were to transcend these teachings, it would distress those people, as it would not be the characteristic of the practice of peaceful bliss.
Second, "nor treating others with contempt" means not relying on the perfect [teachings] to disparage the partial, nor regarding the substantial as important while slighting the provisional.
Third, "not speaking of the long and short of others" first refers to not speaking of any person at all, and subsequently specifically mentions the śrāvakas.

Because a person dislikes hearing of their own faults, they do not speak of others' shortcomings; because they praise someone's face-to-face while criticizing them behind their back, they do not mention their virtues. Furthermore, one should not speak of Zhao’s virtues to Zhang, for Zhao would regard this as using another’s virtues to mock his own shortcomings—a case of using one person to satirize another. Likewise, one must not speak of Zhao’s faults to Zhang, for what is criticized behind Zhao’s back would likewise be criticized behind one’s own. For these reasons, both good and evil are brought to rest.

Furthermore, regarding "not speaking of long or short," the first fascicle of the *Sūryagarbha-sūtra* states: "During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, one should diminish sleep and practice with diligence through seated meditation, reciting sūtras, and cultivating the Way. One turns away from birth and death toward the path of Nirvāṇa; one does not praise the shortcomings of others nor speak of one's own virtues. Being humble, modest, and deferential, one does not act with arrogance or pride. One is content with food and clothing, practices the dhūta ascetic virtues, and exerts oneself without negligence. Fixing the mind in contemplation, one’s thoughts do not wander, and one gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion for all sentient beings."

Furthermore, as described in the sūtras regarding the practice of emptiness: one recites it oneself and teaches others to recite it; one does not slander others, does not speak of their faults, and does not boast of one's own virtues.

Furthermore, as for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle whose spiritual faculties are not yet fixed, if one praises the two vehicles, it may cause them to regress from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Small; if one disparages the two vehicles, it may cause them to lose both the Great and the Small, leaving them with nothing to grasp.

Fourth, regarding "not giving rise to a mind of resentment or aversion": if one thinks that a person’s actions obstruct one’s path, this is a mind of resentment; if one considers them base and inferior, this is a mind of aversion. Once the mental faculty is stirred, speech immediately issues forth. Therefore, by blocking the source of such faults, one does not give rise to resentment or aversion.
The passage beginning with "Practicing well in this manner" refers to the gate of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-mukha*).

Contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena, one’s mind does not grasp or cling, nor does it obstinately adhere [to views]; it neither opposes the intentions of others nor contradicts the characteristics of dharmas (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), and thus one does not answer by teaching the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Regarding the phrase "Answer only with the Mahāyāna": if one perceives that there is no capacity for the Great Vehicle and teaches the Small Vehicle, one gains the benefit of skillful means;
however, if one does not perceive the absence of the Great [capacity] yet teaches the Small, it obstructs the conditions for the Great.
In both cases, this constitutes a failure to perceive [the true capacity]; therefore, to teach only the Great is without fault.
The verse consists of sixteen and a half lines, divided into three parts:
the first two lines are a verse summary of the headings;
the subsequent nine and a half lines are a verse summary of the preceding methods of practice.
The final five lines clarify the accomplishment of practice.
The first two lines of this verse praise the aforementioned "dwelling in the practice of peaceful abiding.
While the preceding section referred to it generally as "one should dwell," these verses specify its distinct characteristics.
There are three aspects of practice:
"teaching the Dharma for peace and security" constitutes half of the practice, meaning one enters the chamber with the desire to enable others to attain the path and its fruit;
"the pure ground" and so forth constitute the other half of the practice, meaning one sits upon the seat.
The single line beginning with "Anointing the body with oil" signifies the meaning of wearing robes.
The three dharmas that guide verbal karma are called "Peaceful Practice.
The nine and a half lines following "Sitting comfortably upon the Dharma-seat" constitute the verses on practice, which are divided into two parts:
The first five and a half lines eulogize the practice of cessation (*śamatha*);
the subsequent four lines eulogize the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the four types of the practice of cessation mentioned above, they are now fully eulogized here.
The first section, "Explaining in Accordance with Questions," consists of half a line; this verse praises the absence of arrogance, for one who is arrogant does not comply.

From "If there is a bhikṣu" to "Answering in accordance with the meaning," there are two and a half lines; these verses praise the avoidance of discussing length or brevity, but rather responding solely according to the meaning without speaking of a person's virtues or faults.
Regarding the statement, "If there are difficult questions, answer them according to the meaning," there are two types:
first, those that can be answered; second, those that cannot be answered.
When questions and answers involve mutual cross-examination and the weighing of relative superiority or inferiority, if one knows for oneself who has won or lost, this is the speech of the wise.
To act with such license as to dare oppose [the ruler] and execute those who do so—this is the speech of a king;
to be ignorant of both long and short, right and wrong, seeking only victory—this is the speech of a fool.

From "Causes, Conditions, and Similes" to "Entering the Buddha-way," spanning three verses and one and a half lines, this section follows up by praising those who do not delight in speaking of the faults of others' persons or teachings.

If one speaks of another's faults, it gives rise to poisonous thoughts in that person; now, by not speaking of their faults, one causes them to resolve to enter the Buddha-way, for the Buddha-way arises from joy.
"Eliminating the mind of indolence" consists of four [verses], one line [each], and praises the absence of resentment and malice.

When a mind of resentment arises, one becomes indolent and afflicted by distress; now, because he preaches the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness, there is no resentment, and thus he is diligent and free from distress.
The preceding prose section explains virtue in terms of *śamatha* (calm abiding), while the verses herein explain virtue in terms of *vipaśyanā* (insightful conduct).
From the passage "Day and night he constantly expounds the unsurpassed Dharma" onwards, the second section consists of four lines that versify the aforementioned gate of contemplation.
Where it was previously stated, "He answers only with the Mahāyāna," the verse says, "Expounding the unsurpassed Way";
where it was previously stated, "Causing them to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)," the verse says, "Vowing to achieve the Buddha-way."
From "I shall enter parinirvāṇa" below, the third section consists of five lines of verse, clarifying the accomplishment of peaceful conduct through speech.
The first line marks the accomplishment of this conduct.

Next, from "Free from envy" below, the second section consists of two lines, clarifying that when there are no internal faults, external difficulties do not arise, just as flies will not come where there is no putrid substance.
Next, from "The wise person is thus" onwards is the third section, consisting of one line, which clarifies that because there are wholesome dharmas within, the practice is accomplished.
Regarding the phrase "As I have explained above": if there are no faults within, it is as explained in the prose;
if there are wholesome qualities within, it is as explained in the verse.
Next, from "The merit of that person" onwards is the fourth section, consisting of one line, which evaluates the merit as per the text.
Third is the Practice of Mental Peace and Bliss, which also includes both prose and verse.
The prose section also consists of three parts:
the presentation of the headings, the explanation of the practices, and the concluding summary.
Within the explanation, there is first cessation (śamatha) and subsequently insight (vipaśyanā).

Within *śamatha* (calm abiding) there are four aspects: first, being free from envy and flattery; second, not disparaging or reviling others; third, not causing disturbance or agitation; and fourth, not engaging in contention.

Now, those of the Two Vehicles who wish to swiftly transcend birth and death first eliminate craving and desire; Bodhisattvas, however, first eliminate anger and [wrong] views. Envy is a defilement of anger, and flattery is a defilement of views. Envy and jealousy contradict the mind of compassion and are not the method for transforming others; flattery and deception deviate from the path of wisdom and are not the method for one's own practice. If wisdom is obstructed, how can one seek the higher goal?
If compassion were to hinder [one's progress], how could one transform others below?
A Bodhisattva practicing the Course of Ease and Bliss must most certainly abandon it.

Regarding the phrase "nor should you revile or scold," one should not use the Perfect Practice to rebuke the Distinct Teaching; one may reprove those who understand their own capacities, but do not scold those who do not. For there is the possibility that such scolding might cause them to lose their roots of goodness.

Regarding the term "bhikṣu" below, one should not apply the universal critique (yuanhe) indiscriminately; since such individuals originally lack the great capacity (da-ji), to forcibly apply the universal critique would contradict their disposition and cause distress. If the universal [teaching] is criticized and the specific (yuan) remains uncomprehended, they will harbor doubts about what preceded and regrets about what followed, losing both the Great and the Small Vehicles.
The path being circuitous is called "very far"; this afflicts those who practice in isolation.
Sinking into emptiness and grasping at realization is called "not attaining"; this afflicts those who practice universally.
Aversion toward birth and death is termed "indolence" (*kausīdya*); the *Karunāpuṣpa Sūtra* clarifies that those of the Hīnayāna are indolent.
From "arousing the mind of great compassion" onwards, the practice of contemplation is explained, which is also fourfold:
initiating the practice of goodness in opposition to the four preceding evils. First, "arousing great compassion for all" opposes envy and flattery.
Second, "arousing the mind of a compassionate father toward the Tathāgata" contradicts reviling and insulting.
Anyone who seeks the Buddha-way is a learner; one must respect the learner as one does the Buddha and must not revile or insult them.
The term "all" (zhū) encompasses the three periods of time; this refers specifically to the Tathāgatas of the future.
Third, "conceiving the thought of a Great Teacher toward Bodhisattvas" is the opposite of causing affliction and disturbance.

The third principle is that those of all three vehicles are equally bodhisattvas; possessing the virtue of transformative instruction, they are all teachers of sentient beings. One should conceive of them as teachers and not speak of their shortcomings.

Fourth is "teaching the Dharma with equanimity": this opposes contentious debate, for it uses equality to dismantle biased attachments and disputes, neither more nor less according to the capacity and acuity of the vessel.
Below the section on "Mañjuśrī," the completion of the practice is summarized in two parts:
first, because evil cannot be inflicted due to the cessation of wrongdoing, it is said that "no one can disturb or afflict" him;
second, because of the practice of contemplation, superior persons gather around him, so that he "obtains good companions in study."
The verse consists of six lines; the first five lines eulogize the two practices of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), each having four points of meaning;
the final line eulogizes the perfection of practice.
Fourth is the vow for the practice of peaceful bliss, which has two parts:
First, the prose exposition; second, the verses.
The prose exposition is further divided into two parts:
first, the clarification of the practice; second, the praise of the sutra.
The practice of the method consists of three parts:
the heading, the method itself, and the conclusion.
The heading is as stated in the text.
The practice of the Dharma consists of three parts:
first, from "Householder and renunciant" onwards, it clarifies the objective of the vow;
second, from "One should form this thought" onwards, it clarifies the reasons for giving rise to the vow.
Third, from the phrase "I shall attain," one proceeds to formally establish the vow. First, the object of the compassionate vow is clarified:

this universally includes those who have previously generated the mind of skillful means but have not yet transcended the triple world, termed "householders," as well as those who have exhausted all pervasive delusions, termed "renunciants. This encompasses both types of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, as well as the three kinds of bodhisattvas; these groups likewise possess ignorance and should thus be objects of great compassion. However, because they have all previously generated the resolve for enlightenment and correspond with the compassionate vow, it is necessary to bestow upon them the bliss of the perfect path and the perfect fruit; therefore, it is said, "one generates a heart of great compassion."
Those who are objects of compassion are not bodhisattvas; this term "non-bodhisattva" refers generally to those who have never yet generated the mind of skillful means (*upāya-citta*).
Since they do not turn toward skillful means at all, how much less so toward reality (*tattva*)?

This compassion encompasses all those within the three realms; these beings must also be granted happiness. However, because their cyclic existence is boundless, it is precisely appropriate to respond with a vow of compassion by uprooting both the causes and effects of their afflictions; thus, it is said that one "generates the mind of great compassion."
From "One should form this thought" up to "preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate," this constitutes the cause for giving rise to compassion.

Because those who delight in the minor [vehicles] take the Buddha’s skillful means to be the ultimate reality and thus fail to encounter the perfect path, it is called a "great loss. This great loss is the cause for the vow of compassion.
Departing from "not hearing and not knowing" is the source of the vow of compassion.

Because one has not yet given rise to the partial or perfect mind, one does not hear the two paths of the partial and the perfect; thus, by not hearing the partial path, one lacks the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); by not knowing it, one lacks the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and by not awakening to it, one lacks the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Furthermore, they lack the threefold wisdom of the perfect and the partial.

Why is this? Because they do not inquire, they do not hear; because they do not believe, they do not know; because they do not understand, they do not practice. Since they lack both the provisional and the real aspects of the threefold wisdom—whether partial or perfect—they are truly to be pitied; this is the reason for the arising of compassion.
From the passage "Even though such a person neither asks about nor believes this sutra" onwards, it concerns the formal making of the vow.

Although that person neither inquires about nor believes in the two paths—the partial (provisional) and the perfect (ultimate)—the Bodhisattva does not make a vow based on the partial path; rather, he desires to bestow upon them the three types of wisdom of the perfect path. Therefore, it is said: "Even though they do not ask about or believe this sutra, once I have attained *sambodhi*, I shall lead them to enter [it]."
Vows, bodhi, wisdom, and supernormal powers are all attained through the practice of peaceful conduct.

Why is this? Because by deeply contemplating the Tathāgata’s seat, one attains the power of wisdom and is adorned with the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), thereby being able to extract [beings] through wisdom.

Profoundly contemplating the Tathāgata’s dwelling and the Tathāgata’s robe, they attain the power of great sublime tranquility; through their supernormal powers and merit, adorned by prior concentration, they manifest various majestic demeanors even while not arising from the meditative absorption of cessation.
From the passage "Departing from Mañjuśrī," the completion of practice is summarized into three parts:
first, the summary that being free from faults constitutes the completion of practice.
How is practice completed?
Because he established the great vow, the practice of entering the Tathāgata’s chamber was perfected;
because he knew the fourfold assembly had lost the perfect path, the practice of the Tathāgata’s seat was perfected;
and because he vowed to restrain his mind so as not to be indolent, the practice of the Tathāgata’s robe was perfected.
Because the three types of conduct are fully established, it is said that "conduct is perfected.

Regarding "being faultless": because compassion is perfected, there is no fault of the stain of anger; because the Tathāgata’s robe is perfected, there is no indolence; and because the Tathāgata’s seat is perfected, there is no deceitfulness.
"Always being a bhikṣu," and so forth, marks the second section: the specific conclusion on the accomplishment of the practice of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Because compassion is accomplished, one receives the offerings and listens to the Dharma from the fourfold assembly and the devas;
because the vow is accomplished, one elicits the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the Buddhas and the protection of the various devas.
The Tathāgata’s seat being established brings joy to the listeners.
From the words "For this reason" onwards is the third section, which explains the fulfillment of the vow and practice.
If even the Buddhas of the three periods protect it, how much more so the devas?
From "Mañjuśrī" down to "this Lotus Sūtra," the second section praises the difficulty of hearing this sūtra.
This is further divided into two parts:
the Dharma-exposition and the parable-exposition.
The discourse on the Dharma is twofold:
first, because it was never previously revealed, one did not obtain it in the past; second, one obtains it only today.
The discourse by way of analogy is likewise twofold:
First, the analogy of not giving the jewel illustrates that it was never previously revealed;
second, the analogy of giving the jewel illustrates that it is heard today.
Each of these two analogies has both an opening and a closing section.
There are six points regarding the analogy of not giving the jewel:

first, subduing all the kingdoms through majesty; second, the subordinate kings being disobedient; third, raising an army to go and punish them; fourth, rejoicing at their success; fifth, bestowing rewards according to their merit; and sixth, not giving them the jewel.

The "Wheel-Turning King" (cakravartin) is likened to the Tathāgata transforming the world; "subduing all kingdoms" is likened to the various objects of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana).
Second, the "minor kings" are likened to the afflictions (kleśa) and so forth; not having attained the subduing power of the untainted (anāsrava), they are said to be "disobedient to his command."

Third, "Raising Various Armies" is a metaphor for the methods within the seven stages of worthiness as the vanguard; the methods within the stages of *srotāpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin* as the middle army; and the methods within the stages of *anāgāmin* and *arhat* as the rearguard.

That which is to be destroyed consists of the eighty-four thousand bandits, such as the three poisons; that which is able to destroy them consists of the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates as the army of officers.

"Below 'The King Sees the Soldiers' is the fourth [section], Rejoicing in Merit. Below "Rewards According to Merit" is the fifth, Rewards According to Merit: "Fields" refers to samādhi; "Dwellings" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*);

"Villages" refer to the first and second fruits (*phala*); "Towns" refer to the third fruit; "Cities" refer to *nirvāṇa*; "Clothing" refers to the wholesome dharmas of shame (*hrī*) and patience (*kṣānti*); "Adornments for the Body" refers to the wholesome dharmas that assist the path; "Various Seven Jewels" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and so forth; "Elephants, Horses, and Carriages" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*) of the two vehicles; "Slaves and Servants" refers to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and possessing impure wholesome dharmas is like having "the populace."
"Only from within the topknot," and so forth, marks the sixth [point]: not bestowing the jewel.

There are those whose faculties are limited to the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*), for whom this constitutes a minor achievement; there are those whose faculties transcend to the realm of transformation (*pariṇāma-vaśitā*), for whom this constitutes a great achievement.

"Startled and amazed" means that when a topknot jewel is suddenly bestowed upon one who has not yet achieved great merit, all the ministers are astonished; likewise, when this sutra is suddenly preached while the great potential of sentient beings has not yet been stirred, those of the two vehicles harbor doubts and the bodhisattvas are startled and amazed.
The six analogies are combined one by one according to the text.
From "Mañjuśrī is like a wheel-turning monarch" onwards, it provides the analogy of the jewel.
This section also has two parts:
First, there is great merit; second, the bestowing of the jewel.

"Bright jewel" means that "bright" is a metaphor for the wisdom of the Middle Way, and "round" is a metaphor for the eternal. "On the crown" signifies that it is the primary object of veneration for the ultimate fruit. "Within the topknot" signifies that the Real is concealed by the Provisional. Untying the topknot is the opening of the Provisional; bestowing the jewel is the revealing of the Real.
The synthesis also consists of two parts:
"enabling one to reach all-knowledge" refers to the fruit, which is the first aspect of practice;
"the foremost teaching" refers to the first aspect of the instruction.
"The Secret Treasury" (Bicang) signifies the oneness of principle, while simultaneously encompassing the oneness of persons.
The verse consists of fourteen and a half lines, divided into two parts:
the first four lines eulogize the superior practice of the Dharma;
The next ten lines and a half eulogize the aforementioned praise of the sutra.
Within the initial eulogy of the practice, there are two parts:
the first line is a transposed eulogy of the accomplishment of the practice.
The preceding section provided a general explanation of the accomplishment of practice; now, the verse specifically clarifies it.
"Constantly practicing patience" refers to the accomplishment of the practice of donning the robes;
"compassionately pitying all beings" refers to the accomplishment of the practice of entering the chamber.
The phrase "is able to expound" praises the accomplishment of the practice of the seat.
Next, from "in the future age" onwards, the second section consists of three lines, praising the method of cultivation.
The first section above consists of three parts—the object, the means, and the vow—which are fully expressed in verse.
Next, from "For example, like one who is powerful" onwards, the second section comprises ten and a half lines of verse, praising the difficulty of hearing this Dharma.
Above, there were [sections on] the Dharma, the Simile, and their Synthesis; now, however, we only provide the verses for the Simile and the Synthesis.
There are two parts to the verses on the Simile:
the first three lines provide the verse for "Not Giving the Jewel."
Next, from "Just as one who is brave" onwards, the second section consists of one verse which bestows the jewel.
Next, from "The Tathāgata is likewise" onwards, the second section correlates the analogy with its meaning.
The first three and a half lines constitute the verse on not giving the jewel;
next, from "Since he knows sentient beings" onwards, the second section consists of three lines, constituting the verse on giving the jewel.
The detailed explanation therein begins with "After my parinirvāṇa" and so forth.

The twenty-three lines below this constitute the third section of this chapter, which summarizes the signs of the attainment of practice and its resulting responses, thereby exhorting one to cultivate the path.
It consists of three parts:
first, one and a half lines, which conclude the exhortation;
next, twenty and a half lines, which cite the three retributions to provide encouragement, also termed the "Purification of the Three Obstructions."
The final line is a summary.

When the three obstacles are purified and transformed, and the evil karma of the present and future lives is exhausted, one immediately attains superior retribution in both the present and future lives.
In the first line, "free from sorrow and affliction" refers to the transformation of the obstacle of retribution (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*), specifically the transformation of present retribution.
Second, the "half-practice" section: "not being born into poverty" refers to the transformation of karmic obstacles (*karmāvaraṇa*), which is the transformation of the retribution of birth.

Third, from "beings delight in seeing [him]" for the following nineteen lines, it refers to the transformation of afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which is the transformation of subsequent retribution.

Now, regarding the first line, "Reading this sutra," it extinguishes the distress and afflictions of the present life; that is, it removes the retribution of painful sensations. This transforms the mind of present retribution, and the absence of illness, pain, and so forth constitutes the transformation of the physical form of retribution.
"May one not be born into poverty": the second section, consisting of half a line, concerns the transformation of evil karma.

While evil karma would normally result in the experience of evil fruits, through the power of this sutra, the evil causes are transformed so that one obtains good fruits; this is precisely the transformation of the retribution of birth.

"Not arising" means that no karma for the production of evil arises; by upholding this sutra in the present life, one does not create the karma for poverty, and thus will not be born into low or base status in future lives.

From the passage "Sentient beings delight in seeing [the Buddha]" onwards, there are nineteen lines which clarify the transformation of subsequent retribution—that is, the transformation of the three afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
It consists of two parts:
first, the initial three practices, which specifically clarify the transformation of the three afflictive hindrances;
second, the sixteen practices, which comprehensively clarify the transformation of all hindrances.
The first section also has three parts.
First, from "Sentient beings delight in seeing [him]" down to one line, the transformation of the obstacle of greed is specifically explained.

Those with excessive desire are treated with contempt by others, and furthermore, this constitutes an obstacle to rebirth in the Brahma heavens; because the obstacle of desire is transformed, he is one whom people delight to see, and celestial youths serve him.
From "Swords and staves cannot be applied" onwards, the second section, consisting of one and a half lines, specifically clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of hatred (*dveṣa*).
By abandoning hatred, one eliminates the internal swords and arrows; by entering the battle array, one is not wounded by external blades.
The second half-verse of "Wisdom-Light" (Prajñā-āloka) consists of three distinct parts, clarifying the transformation of the obstacle of delusion (*moha-āvaraṇa*).

From "If, in a dream, one sees auspicious things" onwards, the second section comprises sixteen lines, which collectively clarify the transformation of all obstacles of affliction (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*); this is also the transformation of subsequent retribution (*paścād-vipāka*).
The manifestation of these signs through the upholding of this sutra should be understood as having been accomplished long ago in the past; they merely arise now by virtue of present conditions.

Furthermore, the various signs regarding the causes and effects of attaining Buddhahood are all "subsequent retributions" (paścātkarma); therefore, one perceives the signs of future subsequent retributions within dreams.

The events of hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas occur within a single thought-moment of dreaming; this serves to manifest that the wondrous Dharma is inconceivable—within the one is the immeasurable, and within the immeasurable is the one. These signs appear before us now, and hereafter they shall surely bear fruit.
Furthermore, there are six [aspects]:

from the initial stage of faith up to the attainment of Buddhahood through the eight phases of manifestation in the state of wondrous enlightenment, one adorns oneself with the adornments of the Tathāgata; this is the retribution of patience.
Approximately the first three lines refer to entering the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) through dreams;

this further divides into two: the first two and a half lines represent the retribution of compassion, while the subsequent half line represents the retribution of right view and freedom from delusion.
Next, from "Furthermore, he sees all Buddhas" onwards, for two sections comprising six lines and a half, is the dream of entering the ten abodes (*bhūmi*).
Next, from "Furthermore, he sees himself situated in... onwards, for three sections comprising three phrases, is the dream of cultivating the ten practices (*caryā*).
Next, from "Realizing all true marks" downward, there are four lines and one phrase, representing the dream-awakening of the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).
Next, from "Deeply entering meditative concentration" downward, there are five and a half lines, representing the dream-entry into the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).
Next, from "The golden bodies of all Buddhas" downward, there are six sections and five lines concerning the dream-entry into wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

Since it states, "Having realized the wisdom of non-retrogression, one is immediately granted a prediction [of Buddhahood]," one should know that this refers to attaining the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), where one receives the prediction through the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
"Furthermore, seeing oneself in the mountains and forests" signifies the cultivation of wholesome dharmas through the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).
"Realizing all true realities" signifies the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), which is the stage of correctly contemplating the Middle Way.

"Entering deeply into meditative concentration" refers to the stainless samādhi within the tenth stage; upon entering the vajra-samādhi, all Buddhas appear before one, bestowing empowerment by stroking the crown of the head.

Dreaming of the Buddha manifesting the eight phases of enlightenment serves to realize wondrous awakening; herein, this likely refers to the sign of being able to achieve Buddhahood through the eight phases at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), which is merely a provisional discourse on ultimate awakening based on the preceding stages.
The single line, "If in a future evil age," summarizes the completion of practice.
As for the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), it is to attain firm faith in the Triple Gem that cannot be undermined by anything;
as for the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*), it is to attain the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).
Through the faculty of mindfulness, one attains the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness;
through the application of diligence, one subdues greed and sorrow;
and through the faculty of concentration, one attains the four dhyānas.
The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is the attainment of the realization of the Four Truths and knowing them as they truly are.
Furthermore, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is the pure faith obtained by generating the bodhicitta toward the Tathāgata;
the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) is the diligence initiated by the mind generated toward the Tathāgata.
The faculty of mindfulness is the mindfulness arising from the resolve for enlightenment directed toward the Tathāgata;
the faculty of concentration is the samādhi arising toward the Tathāgata;
the faculty of wisdom is the wisdom arising toward the Tathāgata.
The Eightfold Right Path is the way of the śramaṇa and is also the dharma of the śramaṇa; the complete exhaustion of greed, hatred, and all afflictions is the meaning of "śramaṇa.
The four fruits are the fruits of the śramaṇa.

Regarding dreams: from the *srotāpanna* up to the *pratyekabuddha*, all have dreams; only the Buddha does not dream, because he is free from doubt and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and thus does not dream.

Dreams arise from five causes, as stated in the verse: through a doubting mind, conceptualization, learning, present circumstances, and the speech of non-human beings—due to these five things there are dreams. Furthermore, there are dreams due to seven things: what has been previously experienced, heard, or seen, as well as various afflictions.
If the present mental consciousness does not yet perceive forms, how can the mental stage (manobhūmi) perceive forms within a dream?
Answer: In all cases, these are merely conceptualizations based on what was previously seen or heard.
Furthermore, these are merely signs of auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
Since one possesses no supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) or knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) within a dream, how could one perceive the affairs of future lives? Answer:
This is not the domain of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna), but rather an inference (anumāna).
It is merely an inference based on the fact that people have previously had such dreams and experienced such results.
Question:
Who sleeps? Answer:
Those in the five destinies as well as those in the intermediate state (antarābhava) all sleep; even those in the womb whose sense faculties are fully developed sleep, and even the Buddha sleeps.
Question:
Sleep is both delusion (*moha*) and a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*); how is this to be reconciled? Answer:
The Buddha arose from his presence because he wished to regulate his body through sleep; this was not the sleep of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) nor the sleep of ignorance (*moha*).

Regarding the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth": the Master is solemn and the Way is honored, and one bows in reverent service. At the single command of the Tathāgata, [the bodhisattvas] rushed forth from the four directions; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth."
His transformative guidance throughout the three periods of time brings boundless benefit; who can fathom the ten thousand reflections of a single moon?
He summons the past to manifest the present and propagates the sutra to benefit the current age; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth."

The void is profound and still, without beginning or end; yet some cling to the traces and remain ignorant of the source. To summon the past to illustrate the present, and to shatter the near to reveal the far, it is therefore said: "The Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth."

The youth at the site of tranquility (Śīlamaṇḍa) and the aged child of tranquil light (Śīmaprabhāsa) demonstrate the power of their medicinal roots so that all may come to know it; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth.

The text asks, "From where have they come, and by what causes and conditions have they gathered? Now, by explaining this chapter through various meanings to reveal the understanding of the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas*, it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth."
The following is the second major section, which reveals the immediate traces of the Master’s school and manifests the distant origin of the Buddha-ground.
This text consists of three parts:
first, from this point down to "You yourselves shall, by means of this, come to hear it," is the introductory section;
2. From "At that time, Śākyamuni addressed Maitreya" down to the nineteen verses spoken by Maitreya in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit," this is the section of the formal exposition;
3. From after the verses down through eleven and a half chapters, this is the section of the dissemination, and so forth.
The introduction consists of two parts:
first, the emergence; second, the inquiry.
The emergence consists of three parts:
First, the bodhisattvas from other directions request that the sutra be propagated; second, the Tathāgata does not grant permission; third, they leap forth from the lower direction.
Having heard that the merit of transmitting the sutra is vast, the bodhisattvas from other directions all desire to make vows to dwell here and propagate it, and thus they request him to do so.
The Tathāgata’s reasons for halting [this teaching] are threefold:
first, each of you has your own specific duties; if you remain in this land, you would neglect the benefit of others there.

Second, the conditions for establishing karmic connections between that other region and this land are shallow; even if one were to preach and transmit [the teachings] here, there would certainly be no great benefit. Third, [the third reason follows].

Furthermore, if one were to grant this [position], then it would be impossible to summon those below; if those below do not come, the traces cannot be destroyed and the distant cannot be revealed. These are the three points for which the Tathāgata has refuted [this view].
There are three meanings for summoning those from the lower regions:

first, these are my disciples who ought to propagate my Dharma; second, because their conditions are profound and vast, they are able to bring benefit throughout this land, throughout all lands where they manifest their bodies, and throughout lands in other directions; third, it serves to reveal the distant by opening up the near. For these reasons, he remains there while summoning those from below.
From the passage "At that time the Buddha said" onwards is the third section; the emergence from below is divided into two parts:
first, the narrator’s description of the signs, and second, the inquiry after their well-being.
Each section has five parts.
The first five are: first, emerging;
second, physical characteristics; third, dwelling place; fourth, receiving the command; and fifth, retinue.

The dwelling place is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light. "Constant" refers to the virtue of permanence; "quiescent" refers to the virtue of bliss; "light" refers to purity and selfhood. This constitutes the secret treasury of the four virtues, which is its dwelling place; it dwells within this secret treasury by means of the dharma of non-dwelling.
"Below" refers to the abyssal depths of the Dharma-nature and the ultimate ground of the profound mystery; hence it is called "below.
It does not belong to this world when situated below, nor does it belong to that world within space; being neither this nor that is precisely the Middle Way.
Emerging from this, it is not above, nor is it below; abiding neither above nor below in the midst of space, it is likewise the Middle Way.

As for the reasons for its coming: it comes because it has heard the mandate, it comes to propagate the Dharma, it comes to shatter attachments, and it comes to reveal the fundamental nature—all as explained above.

Regarding the retinues they lead: if one judges according to common human expectations, those leading sixty thousand or fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands] are considered many, while those leading three, two, or one are considered few, and those who are alone are considered solitary.
However, if one seeks this according to the text, those with sixty thousand or fifty thousand are considered few, while those who are alone are considered many.

The text states that those who dwell alone and solitary are actually more numerous than the aforementioned; yet if one relies upon the Dharma-gates, each and every one is the virtue of the Teacher, capable of leading all people to the place of treasure. One should know that "one" is not truly solitary, and "sixty thousand" is not truly many. "One" refers to the single path of purity; "two" refers to concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*); "three" refers to precepts, concentration, and wisdom; "four" refers to the Four Noble Truths; "five" refers to the five eyes; and "six" refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Each perfection encompasses the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), and within each realm there are ten; ten makes a hundred, and a hundred possesses a thousand. Ten wholesome deeds make ten thousand; thus, one perfection possesses ten thousand, and the six perfections constitute sixty thousand Dharma-gates. Many are not many, and one is not few. It is neither many nor few, yet it is both many and few, and so forth.
From the passage "These bodhisattvas emerged from the earth" onwards is the second section, the inquiry after their well-being, which consists of five parts:

first, offerings of the three karmas; second, the words of the inquiry; third, the Buddha’s response regarding their peace and happiness; fourth, verses of sympathetic joy; and fifth, the Tathāgata’s praise.

Regarding the offering made during the first three watches of the night, which lasted fifty minor kalpas yet was perceived by the fourfold assembly as being like half a day—this is an instance of concealing the long to manifest the short; by borrowing his supernatural power, he caused what is narrow to appear vast. Both of these are inconceivable.
"Circumambulation" refers to the body; "praising the Dharma" refers to speech; and "gazing up with reverence" refers to the mind.
As for the "fifty intermediate kalpas" and the "half-day," these are inconceivable in terms of time.

That which the Tathāgata perceives is not by means of dualistic characteristics; the Bodhisattvas from the lower regions constantly extol him face-to-face, and the Tathāgata silently accepts their praise. To those who understand, what is short is made long—meaning fifty minor kalpas; to those who are deluded, what is long is made short—meaning as little as half a day. This serves as a preliminary lead-in for the distinction between the fundamental and the manifested.
Before the Tathāgata had spoken, people were shrouded in darkness regarding the fundamental and clung to the superficial;
once the Buddha revealed and clarified it, they awakened to what was near and reached what was far, thereby realizing that the inconceivable is one and the same.
That the fourfold assembly perceives the Bodhisattva everywhere is likewise inconceivable.

For what is seen by the fleshly eye and the divine eye does not extend far; yet now that which is beheld fills the void of space. Seeing the rain fall so violently, one knows the dragon is great; seeing the flowers flourish so profusely, one knows the pond is deep. Seeing him pervade the entirety of space, one knows he is truly equal to the Dharma-realm.
First, the four guides are designated;
second, the words of inquiry are set forth.
The inquiry consists of two parts:
The prose and the verses.
The prose has two parts:
first, inquiring after the Tathāgata’s well-being; second, inquiring whether sentient beings are easy to deliver, and so forth.

The reason only four individuals are mentioned is intended to illustrate the forty stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, just as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* mentions only Dharmamati, Guṇakara, Suvarṇadhvaja, and Suvarṇagarbha when explaining these forty stages, and so forth.
Third, the Tathāgata answers fully.
The two matters of being at ease and being easy to deliver are mutually constitutive: being easy to deliver means being at ease, and being at ease means being easy to deliver.
Being easy to deliver is twofold:

First, there are those with sharp faculties and profound merit who, throughout successive lifetimes, have constantly received the Great Transformation; upon first seeing my body, they immediately receive the *Avataṃsaka* and enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Their fruit is ripe and easily shed, and thus these sentient beings are easy to deliver.

Second, there are those with dull faculties and meager merit who, throughout successive lifetimes, have not received the Great Transformation; for the sake of such people, it is necessary to open the path of gradual teaching for the dull-witted—using the Tripiṭaka, the Vaipulya, and the *Prajñāpāramitā*—to subdue them, so that even these individuals may now hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and enter the Buddha’s wisdom.

Although this is more difficult than what preceded it, it is extremely easy for the Buddha, for the Buddha recognizes what is appropriate and attains the proper means; with slight application of ointment and cauterization, their awakening through wisdom is identical. Now, ten points will be briefly raised to explain it: First, the initial vision versus the present vision;

second, opening and closing versus not opening and closing; third, vertical expansion versus horizontal brevity; fourth, the one fundamental versus the many traces, and the shared trace versus the solitary fundamental; fifth, added explanation versus non-added explanation; sixth, transformation of the land versus non-transformation of the land; seventh, multiple locations versus a single location; eighth, refutation and supersession versus non-refutation and non-supersession; ninth, directly revealing the real and opening up the provisional to reveal the real; tenth, those of sharp faculties maturing first versus those of dull faculties maturing later.
Regarding "first seen" and "now seen": when he first attained the Way, it was called "first seen"; at the long subsequent assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the ultimate reality is called "now seen.
The sun shining upon the high mountain represents the teaching of the sudden (*tun*), which is neither opened nor closed;
for those who have not yet entered, the sudden is opened to explain the gradual (*jian*), using the five flavors to subdue them so that they may gradually return to the sudden.

Because one enters directly and vertically into the Dharma-realm, it is called "vertical breadth"; because one does not pass through gradual expedients, it is called "horizontal brevity. Now, passing through the five flavors is "horizontal breadth," and attaining entry into the Buddha-wisdom is likewise "vertical breadth."

The single platform is the original essence, hence it is one; the thousand petals are the manifested traces, hence they are many. Because the traces are identical to all other sutras, they are called "shared"; because the original essence differs from all other sutras, it is called "unique."
Adding the four Bodhisattvas, forty stages are taught; [the Buddha] himself speaks of the opening, showing, awakening, and entering, without adding these to others.
Because it is the Flower King World (*Puṣpakūṭa*), it is said to be "unchanging"; because the two lands are transformed, it is said to be "transforming the land."
The seven locations and eight assemblies constitute many places; however, because Vulture Peak Mountain is situated far out in space, it does not constitute many places.
The destruction of the conjured city and the alteration of the hired laborers are described as "expulsion" and "seizure"; since such things do not occur here, there is no expulsion or seizure.
Practicing the great, direct path is called "revealing the real through the direct"; definitively resolving the Śrāvaka teachings is called "opening the provisional to reveal the real.
Those with sharp faculties whose conditions have matured enter the Buddha-wisdom at the outset; those with dull faculties who mature later enter the Buddha-wisdom now.

The conditions and suitability [of these beings] differ, which can be summarized as ten distinctions. Because the seed-knowledge (*jñāna*) and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are without differentiation, the text states: "Upon first seeing my body and hearing what I preach, they all immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata—except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna."
"Now, regarding this sutra, one enters the Buddha’s wisdom; the clear evidence is right here, so there is no need for doubt.

Various masters, seeing that the conditions differ, follow those differing conditions with divergent interpretations; thus they remain lost and fail to return, drifting further and further from the Way. If one recognizes that the principle is the same—like a thousand chariots sharing the same ruts—the Buddha’s wisdom is without distinction."

The former [tradition] stated that the *Avataṃsaka* is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), possesses the full letters (*pūrṇākṣara*), and is eternal; whereas the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*), lacks the full letters, and is not eternal. Now, comparing these texts together: if entering [the path] at the beginning was of definitive meaning, then entering it now is of non-definitive meaning; if entering at the beginning was the Buddha’s wisdom (*buddhajñāna*), then entering now is not the Buddha’s wisdom. If the Buddha’s wisdom is already equal to the definitive meaning, then the full letters and the eternal must likewise be so, and so forth.

The people of this land call the *Avataṃsaka* the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* the Not-Perfect Teaching (*buzhenzong*); here, too, we employ this text to treat them as equal.
Fourth, the Bodhisattvas’ understanding and sympathetic rejoicing (*anumodanā*).

Those capable of questioning are the four great bodhisattvas in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and Śāriputra’s three requests in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*; all of these are examples of those capable of questioning.
That which is asked is precisely a question regarding the Buddha’s wisdom.
Fifth, as for the Tathāgata’s praise and exhortation, it differs significantly from the question; the questioner rejoices in it.
Those who are able to ask such questions are all bodhisattvas, and those who have been transformed by them hear this and practice it with faith; we rejoice in this.
When the Tathāgata praises the one who has performed the transformation and expresses his own rejoicing, what is the meaning of this?

However, those who are able to ask such questions are all ancient Buddhas; that you are able to rejoice in this is itself the Tathāgata. Bodhisattvas rejoice in its traces, while the Tathāgata praises its source. This, too, is a secret indication of the lifespan, and so forth.
"Then Maitreya and the eighty thousand great beings... and so forth, marks the second section: the introduction of the inquiry.

From the time of the Śākyamuni Buddha’s descent from the site of enlightenment until the present assembly, the great beings from the ten directions have come to this gathering without interruption; though they are beyond limit, I—by the power of my wisdom as a Bodhisattva in his final birth—see and know them all. Yet, among this multitude, I do not recognize a single person. Furthermore, as I travel through the ten directions to pay homage to the Buddhas, I am well known to the great assemblies of those Buddhas; yet even at the places where I have traveled, I am not recognized. Whether coming or going, when I investigate it in this way, I am not recognized by anyone.

Furthermore, those great beings (mahāsattvas) are pioneers who have gone before, whereas Maitreya is a junior student of a later generation; because the latter does not know the former, he does not recognize them.

Moreover, those great beings have, from the very beginning, reached the bottom of the true mark (lakṣaṇa) and manifested throughout the ten directions; their respective teachings as true and responsive bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are beyond the realm of Maitreya, and for this reason, he does not recognize them.

Furthermore, the Buddha, entrusting the propagation of the sutra, summoned the great bodhisattvas; these bodhisattvas came because they heard their master’s command. They secretly heard of the lifespan [of the Buddha], yet as it was not something known by the assembly at that time, they said they did not know it.
This is an explanation of the introductory section concerning doubts and questions based on the four *siddhāntas*, and so forth.
There are two types of doubts and questions:
first, the doubts of bodhisattvas in this land; second, the doubts of bodhisattvas in other lands.
There are two further doubts regarding this land:
first, the doubt expressed in the prose;
second, the formal inquiry in nineteen and a half verses, which is further divided into five parts:
The first line and phrase inquire from where [they] have come;
next, from "By what causes and conditions" onwards, the second section consists of one line and three phrases, inquiring by what causes and conditions they have come;
next, from "Each and every bodhisattva" onwards, the third section consists of nine lines, describing their number.
Next, from "These ones of great majesty and virtue" onwards is the fourth section, consisting of two lines, which asks who their teacher is;
next, from "Such supernatural powers of the bodhisattvas" onwards is the fifth section, consisting of five and a half lines, which concludes the request. This is further divided into five parts:
first, the initial two lines conclude with an expression of praise.
Next, following "The earth in the four directions," is the second section consisting of two lines, requesting an answer as to the place of origin;
next, following "I, among this assembly," is the third section consisting of one line, requesting an answer as to the cause for coming;
next, following "Now, this great assembly," is the fourth section consisting of one and a half lines, where the entire gathering makes a collective request.
Next, following "Immeasurable Virtue" (*apramāṇaguṇa*), the fifth section consists of two lines concerning the request for a response from the Master of the Assembly, and so forth.

Second, regarding the bodhisattvas from other lands who harbor doubts: their manifested bodies and retinues are distributed throughout the ten directions, and they share the same doubts as Maitreya; both groups do not know the original ground [of Śākyamuni], wishing to manifest that his attainment of enlightenment was extremely long ago. Each has presented their doubts to the Buddha, and the Buddha has suppressed them all while awaiting Maitreya, and so forth.
From "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya" onwards is the second section: the actual exposition (*bhāṣya*).
This text is divided into two parts:
first, the prose (*gadya*); second, the verses (*śloka*), which consist of the preliminary instructions and permissions, followed by the actual exposition.
The prose section first provides a praise;
next, it offers an admonition, exhorting one not to be distracted, not to be indolent, and not to retreat;
following this, it grants permission and indicates the wisdom of the fruit, wherein "wisdom of the fruit" refers to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision—the sublime fruit of knowledge and vision.
Next, regarding "teaching through transformation," it means "proclaiming and manifesting.

"Mastery of supernatural powers" refers to benefiting sentient beings in the past; "the lion’s vigorous leap" refers to the places where the emanated bodies reach throughout the ten directions in the present.
Some say that "fury" (*visphūrjita*) refers to the state of being about to advance; this signifies the aspect of remaining eternally in the future to benefit sentient beings.
As for "great power and majesty," this refers to benefiting beings in the future.
Alternatively, one may take this as referring to the present shaking of the ten directions, according to the intended application of the meaning.
It would be best, however, to follow the sequence of the text.
Furthermore, I privately maintain that "the sovereign power of the Tathāgata" refers to myself.
"Supernormal powers" (abhijñā) signify bliss;
"lion’s bound" (siṃhavikrīḍita) signifies the purification achieved through vigorous exertion to remove defilements;
and "great power and majesty" signifies the constant benefit of beings in the future, which is permanence.
This refers to the meaning of the four virtues, and so forth.
Regarding the four stanzas of verse: the first three lines praise the three admonitions;
the final three lines and one phrase praise the granting of permission.
The first line of verse praises and indicates the fruit of wisdom;
the following three lines praise the three periods of time.
From "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards is the second section, which constitutes the actual exposition.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, from this point up to the end of the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*), it primarily elucidates the near while revealing the distant;
second, at the beginning of the "Chapter on Distinction" (*Vibhaṅga-parivarta*), there is the general bestowal of the prediction of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Third, Maitreya’s general summary of his understanding and realization.
This section has two parts:

first, briefly opening up the near to reveal the distant, thereby moving fixed attachments and giving rise to doubt; second, extensively opening up the near to reveal the distant, thereby severing delusions and generating faith.
Briefly, there are two parts: first, the brief exposition; second, the further request due to doubt.

Regarding the brief exposition, there are both prose and verse; herein, only the two questions are answered, while the question regarding the causes and conditions for their assembly is not answered. Because it is not answered, a further request is made. The prose provides a dual response and a dual explanation as found in the text.
Regarding those who dwell in the space below, the *Śāstra* clarifies that there is the *atibhū-samādhi* (the samādhi of transcending the base). This should be explained in four ways:

first, "existence" (*yu*) refers to the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*), while "base" (*di*) refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naiva-saṃjñā-nāsaṃjñāyatana*); it is called the "base" because it is profound and supreme.
Furthermore, "existence" refers to names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), while "base" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); it is called the "base" because it is empty and quiescent.
Furthermore, there are those who hold that the "two sides" refer to the mundane world, while the "bottom" refers to the fulfillment of ultimate wisdom.

In this present sutra, however, the space below is taken as the bottom; it is neither the upper realm nor the lower realm, but represents the Middle Way as the bottom. This is an analysis according to the teachings, and so forth.
