The passage beginning with "In all the sūtras" is the commentary.

The Master knew that his disciple was fully endowed with the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*); first, he practiced both wisdom and abandonment together, and subsequently, he realized both wisdom and abandonment together.

Discriminating among the sūtras is the cultivation of knowledge; right mindfulness is the cultivation of abandonment; not delighting in the assembly is the realization of abandonment; and diligent application of effort is the realization of knowledge.
"Abiding without relying on humans or devas" is the explanation of the locus.
Humans and devas constitute the two extremes; it means not dwelling in and not clinging to them.
"Profound wisdom without obstruction" refers to reliance upon inconceivable wisdom.
"Delighting in the Buddha-dharma" means delighting in the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).
Since both the realm and its corresponding wisdom are extremely subtle, this is not the domain of bodhisattvas who practice only proximate cultivation.
Of the eight and a half verses, the first five and a half verses provide a verse-by-verse response to the two questions; the final three verses provide a dual explanation, and so forth.
From "At that time, Maitreya" onwards, [the text] further requests [an explanation] due to doubt.
It consists of prose and verse.
The prose section is divided into two parts:

I. Doubt; II. Inquiry. Having heard the former statement that "under the Bodhi tree they were taught and now all abide in non-retrogression," and having also heard the statement that "I have been teaching these multitudes since long ago," they were moved by these two accounts and gave rise to doubt based on their attachments.
From the phrase "He addressed the Buddha" onwards, there are two further sections where he raises doubts and requests further instruction:
first, the teaching by way of principle (*dharma*), and second, the teaching by way of analogy (*upamā*). The teaching by way of principle is divided into three parts:

First, from "He then addressed the Buddha" onwards, there is (1) the doubt that because those converted during the recent period of attaining enlightenment are so numerous, one clings to the proximity [of the time] and doubts the distance [of the duration];

next, from "World-Honored One, these great bodhisattvas" onwards, there is (2) the second [doubt]: since those converted are so numerous and their stages of practice are profound and subtle, one clings to the distance [of the duration] and doubts the proximity [of the time];
next, from "World-Honored One, such a matter as this" onwards, there is (3) the concluding request.
The parable contains both opening and closing sections.
It opens into three parts:
"His complexion is beautiful and his hair is black" illustrates the sense that his attainment of the Way was imminent.
"Pointing to a hundred-year-old man" and departing from him is a metaphor for the meaning that those transformed [by the Buddha] are exceedingly numerous.

The various masters of the region east of the Huai River explain this metaphor by means of another metaphor: suppose a father takes an elixir that restores youth, and his appearance becomes identical to that of a twenty-five-year-old, while his son does not take the medicine and his form remains like that of a hundred-year-old. Those who know the power of the medicine would not doubt the relationship between father and son; those who do not know it would find it strange.

Likewise, the Tathāgata has taken the medicine of manifesting traces and showed himself born at Gayā, while the various Bodhisattvas speak directly of their original ground—having long ago resolved upon the Way and now abiding in non-retrogression. If the Buddha and the Buddhas thoroughly understand this matter, those below them cannot reach such understanding and thus cannot help but harbor doubts.
The passage beginning with “This matter is difficult to believe” concludes the analogy.
First, the near analogy is combined with the text as it appears;
from “And yet this great assembly” onwards, the distant analogy is combined.
Observe that this Bodhisattva has long planted roots of goodness; his resolve did not arise merely at Gayā. Regarding "skillfully entering, emerging, and abiding":

the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) constitute skillful entry; the lion’s sport (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*) constitutes skillful emergence; and the leap-over (*vyutkrāntaka*) constitutes skillful abiding—this is the general meaning.

Alternatively, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) to the tenth is called skillful entry; entering the gate of profound mystery from the tenth stage and practicing the affairs of ordinary beings in reverse order is called skillful emergence; and the pervasive perfection of wondrous enlightenment is called skillful abiding—this is the specific meaning.

The samādhi of the ultimate nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is called "skillful entry"; the Śūraṅgama is called "skillful emergence"; and the King Samādhi is called "skillful abiding. This refers to the perfection of the intention.

Practicing various wholesome dharmas in succession constitutes "skillful practice" from the perspective of the cause, while it is termed "skillful entry" from the perspective of the fruit, and so forth.
"Skillfully answering difficult questions" refers to being endowed with the two types of adornment.
Because he is the honored one among the seven stages of expedient means, he is called a "Jewel.
From the words "Today, the World-Honored One" onwards is the request for an answer; this section also has three parts, beginning from "Today," which cites the Buddha's words.
From "We [pray]" onwards, secondly, the intention of the request is clarified.
This intention of the request is twofold:
first, for the sake of those in the present.
"Although I have not yet attained [realization], I shall simply believe.
From the passage "However, as for the various bodhisattvas" onwards is the second section, concerning the future.

Those of shallow practice easily give rise to slander; those who have newly resolved their minds fall into evil realms through their slandering. While those who are non-retrogressive may believe and do not slander, they are unable to increase their progress on the Path.
"If [the teaching] is analyzed, those who slander it will give rise to faith, and those with faith will increase their progress on the Path," and so forth.
From "So be it" onwards is the third section: the request for an answer.
The response also consists of two parts:
first, "dispelling our doubts";
second, from "and for the sake of the future" onwards, dispelling the doubts of the future.
The fourteen verses of the gāthā eulogize the preceding [sections on] the Dharma and the parable:
five lines eulogize the discourse on the Dharma, and nine lines eulogize the discourse on the parable.
Within the discourse on the Dharma, there are three parts:
The first line constitutes the first section, praising the proximity [of the Buddhas];
next, from "These sons of the Buddha" onwards, the second section consists of two lines and three phrases, praising the doubt regarding their distance;
finally, from "How could it be possible" onwards, the third section consists of one line and one phrase, praising the concluding request.
In the verses of the analogy, the first two lines correspond to the opening of the analogy;
the subsequent seven lines beginning with "The World-Honored One is also like this" correspond to the application of the analogy.
This section also has three parts:
The first two lines of the verse correspond to the proximate [cause];
next, from "These bodhisattvas, with equal resolve" onwards, the second section consists of three and a half lines, which correspond to the remote [cause];
finally, from "We have heard this from the Buddha" onwards, the third section consists of three lines, which correspond to the request for a response, and so forth.
The Wenshu (Textual Commentary) on the Lotus Sutra, Fascicle Nine, Part One.
